statement: In published cases of cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (bouts of severe nausea and vomiting, again and again, in people who use cannabis regularly), pooled descriptively in a systematic review of reports from 2000 to September 2015 (Sorensen et al., 2017; AMSTAR 2 critically low; 211 patients from 80 case reports and 7 case series, 98 of them from one series entered as summary figures; no randomized trials, no comparison groups and no count of how many people who use cannabis develop the syndrome), all patients had recurrent vomiting with severe nausea and 85.1% had abdominal pain; 154 of 211 (72.9%) were men; among the 113 patients with individual data, the median age was 16 at first cannabis use (IQR 14 to 18; 84 patients), 24 at the start of symptoms (19 to 29; 101) and 28 at diagnosis (22 to 34; 111). Of the 197 whose frequency of use was reported, 76.6% used cannabis daily or more often and 97.4% at least weekly (the reviewers counted reports of heavy use as daily and of frequent use as weekly), and 45 of 179 (25.1%) had used for a year or less before symptoms began. Of the patients whose bathing was reported, 157 of 170 (92.3%) found that hot baths or showers relieved their symptoms. Of the 64 patients whose stopping was documented, 62 (96.8%) had complete resolution of symptoms; the two without resolution had no urine test to confirm that they had stopped, and all 21 patients who kept using still had symptoms. The review's tables differ on the details: its main table counts relief after abstinence or reduction and places one of the two patients without resolution in a case series rather than in the case reports the text cites, and another table describes a patient in the 98-patient series who did not improve despite reported abstinence, a patient the main table leaves out of the count. Follow-up was documented for only 85 of the 211 patients (40.2%), no time to resolution is reported although it was among the data to be collected, and whether symptoms returned when people started again was too inconsistently documented to count, although in one series all 3 patients who used cannabis again after a period without it became ill again. The review proposes recognising the syndrome by severe cyclic vomiting, usually with abdominal pain, at least weekly cannabis use before symptoms began, temporary relief with hot bathing and resolution after stopping, with male sex, starting cannabis in the teenage years and symptoms beginning in the twenties as supporting features; these features come from cases diagnosed by them, so their frequencies do not show how well they separate the syndrome from other causes of repeated vomiting, which no study in the review tested. In second-hand surveys of patients diagnosed with cyclic vomiting syndrome, 72% of 31 and 67% of 437 also used hot showers for relief, although many of them used cannabis (42% daily to weekly in the first; 81% in the second). Diagnosis came on average 4.1 years (SD 4.6) after symptoms began, and in four case reports patients first diagnosed with severe vomiting of pregnancy, whose cyclic vomiting had begun before the pregnancy, were later diagnosed with the syndrome. A 2021 review says the distinction from other cyclic vomiting disorders is underdeveloped and gives 90% of patients as reporting that hot baths and stopping cannabis relieve their symptoms, citing a 2019 clinical review and Sorensen et al. (2017) itself and merging two features that the systematic review counts separately (Connor et al., 2021; second-hand), and a 2014 review links repeated use with increased vomiting without a citation (Volkow et al., 2014). All nine proposed mechanisms were rated very low, and three cases involved synthetic cannabinoids; acute hospital treatments are covered in the claims on capsaicin cream and on dopamine-blocking medicines. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Cannabis hyperemesis syndrome means bouts of severe nausea and vomiting, usually with belly pain, in people who use cannabis regularly. In 211 published cases, about three in four used cannabis daily or more, but a quarter had used it for a year or less before the bouts began, and most found that hot baths or showers eased the symptoms for a while, though many people with other kinds of repeated vomiting use hot showers too. Of the 64 cases where stopping was recorded, 62 got completely better, and the 21 people who kept using did not. These are published cases only: nobody knows from them how common the syndrome is, fewer than half of the cases had any follow-up written down, and the signs used to recognise it come from the same cases, so how well they tell it apart from other vomiting illnesses has not been tested. On average it took about 4 years from the first symptoms to the diagnosis.
population: Patients with a clinician's diagnosis of cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome described in published case reports and case series, 2000 to 2015 (211 patients; 72.9% men; median age at diagnosis 28)
exposure: Regular cannabis use as reported in each case (frequency known for 197, duration for 179); three cases involved synthetic cannabinoids
comparator: None (case descriptions); for resolution, patients who stopped compared with those who kept using
outcome: Features of the syndrome as recorded; relief with hot bathing; resolution of symptoms after stopping cannabis
magnitude: Sorensen 2017 cumulative synthesis (211 patients; each share is of the patients in whom the feature was reported): recurrent vomiting 100% (211); severe nausea and vomiting 100% (211); abdominal pain 85.1% (202); relief with hot bathing 92.3% (157 of 170); resolution after stopping 96.8% (62 of 64; all 21 who kept using had ongoing symptoms); at least weekly use 97.4% (197); daily or more 76.6% (197); regular use for more than a year 74.8% (179); men 72.9% (154 of 211). Duration of use before onset (179): 1 year or less 25.1%, 2-5 years 36.3%, 6-10 years 16.8%, 11 years or more 21.8%. Median ages, from the 113 patients with individual data: first use 16 (IQR 14-18; 84), onset 24 (19-29; 101), diagnosis 28 (22-34; 111). Mean delay to diagnosis 4.1 years (SD 4.6). Follow-up documented for 85 of 211 (40.2%). One series: all 3 patients who resumed after abstinence relapsed. Second-hand, cyclic vomiting syndrome surveys: hot showers used by 72% of 31 (42% using cannabis daily to weekly) and 67% of 437 (81% using cannabis).

evidence.extracted: MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science and Cochrane, January 2000 to 24 September 2015, English only, plus grey literature: 170 articles included (183 in the abstract), with case reports (8 excluded) and 8 case series of four or more patients; no randomized trials of diagnosis, mechanism or treatment; study quality too low for meta-analysis.

risk_of_bias.note: Published case reports and series chosen by clinicians who decided to report them, often cases resembling the first description; the features counted are those used to make the diagnosis; outcomes documented for a minority (stopping for 64, any follow-up for 85 of 211) and abstinence not verified; no risk-of-bias tool applied by the review (card sc_sorensen_2017, AMSTAR 2 critically low).

inconsistency.note: The case reports and series describe the same features; some series' numbers differ between the review's text and tables (card reporting issues), which does not change the picture.

indirectness.note: Published, mostly hospital-diagnosed cases cannot stand for everyone who develops the syndrome, and the case features answer how it is recognised only as descriptions, not as tested diagnostic criteria.

imprecision.note: Not downgraded separately; the floor is reached.

publication_bias.note: Selection into publication is counted under risk of bias.

grade.reasoning: Case reports and series are observational and start low; down two levels for risk of bias (selection, circular diagnosis, incomplete follow-up) and one for indirectness: very low, the floor. Status replicated: the same picture (recurrent vomiting with regular use, relief with hot water, resolution after stopping) comes from many case reports and several series by different teams, though they reach the claim through one review and the series inside it are not counted again (card sc_sorensen_2017). Connor et al. (2021) take their 90% from a 2019 clinical review and from Sorensen et al. (2017) itself, so it is not separate evidence. The resolution figure describes documented cases, not what happens to everyone who stops, and the review's own tables differ on its details.
